passage:
Dear Shreya didi,
Today was a whole year in one day. Morning: someone I like on the school bus smiled at me and I felt like I could fly. Noon: Sir punished our whole row for talking when it was only two boys, and I was so angry I shook. I nearly threw my bottle. Evening: I came home and cried in the bathroom for no reason I could explain, just this heavy grey feeling.
Is this normal? It scares me how fast it changes.
I told Mummy a bit at dinner. She didn't laugh. She said she felt like this at sixteen too, and that if the grey stays a long time or feels too heavy, we'll talk to the school counsellor together.
Write back?
Baljeet

qa.q: What did Sir do at noon?
qa.a: Sir punished the whole row for talking when it was only two boys.

qa.q: What worries Baljeet most about the day?
qa.a: Baljeet is scared by how fast the feelings change, from flying to shaking with anger to a heavy grey sadness.

qa.q: What choice did Baljeet make that evening, and how did Mummy respond?
qa.a: Baljeet told Mummy a bit at dinner; she listened without laughing, said she felt this way at sixteen and offered to see the school counsellor together if the grey stays long or feels too heavy.

qa.q: How might Shreya didi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She may feel trusted and want to reassure Baljeet that these swings are common, while backing Mummy's plan.

grounding: Shows a teenager swinging from a crush to rage at unfairness to deep sadness in one day, and a steady adult who listens and keeps help in reach.

passage:
Nirmala Masi, can I just talk and you don't fix anything? Okay. This morning I was so happy I sang in the shower, because the drama club picked my script. Then at lunch I found out Pooja was left out of the trip because her fees were late, and I was furious, like, burning. I wrote a whole speech in my head for the principal. And by four o'clock I was lying on my bed feeling like nothing matters and nobody likes me.
Three different people in one day, Masi. Is something wrong with me?
You felt like this too? Really? At my age? 'It gets steadier, Tanuja,' you say. Okay. I believe you.
Can I sit here a while? Your kitchen is quieter than my head.

qa.q: Why was Pooja left out of the trip?
qa.a: Because her fees were late.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling by four o'clock?
qa.a: Tanuja felt low and flat, as if nothing matters and nobody likes Tanuja.

qa.q: What choice did Tanuja make that helped with the swings?
qa.a: Tanuja chose to go to Nirmala Masi and talk without asking to be fixed, finding a steady adult and a quiet kitchen.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Masi feel when Tanuja asks 'Is something wrong with me?'
qa.a: Masi may feel tender and protective, and want Tanuja to know such swings are common, as she seems to have shared from her own teenage years.

grounding: Shows a teenager feeling joy, rage at unfairness and sadness in one day, and turning to a steady adult who listens.

passage:
Aditi,
I have to tell someone about Tuesday, and you're the only one who won't laugh. Morning: Imran smiled at me in the corridor, and I was floating till second period. Then in chemistry Ma'am blamed me for the beaker that Saira broke, and I was so angry I shook. I nearly screamed at her. By evening I was crying on my bed over nothing: a song, the rain, I don't even know. Ammi came and sat with me, didn't ask anything, just rubbed my back. She said she used to feel like a weather report too at fifteen. It helped. Do you ever feel like this? Tell me I'm not the only one.
Hafsa

qa.q: Who broke the beaker?
qa.a: Saira.

qa.q: How did Hafsa's feelings change through Tuesday?
qa.a: Hafsa went from floating with joy to shaking with anger to crying with sadness, all in one day.

qa.q: What did Ammi do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with Hafsa, rubbed her back without questioning and said she had felt the same at that age.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel receiving this letter?
qa.a: Aditi would probably feel trusted and close, and may recognise the same highs and lows.

grounding: Shows a teen swinging from a crush to rage to sadness in one day, steadied by a calm parent.

passage: Honestly, being fifteen is exhausting. I'm Anand, and last Saturday alone I went from the best morning of my life, scoring in the inter-school final, to wanting to punch a wall at lunch because the ref gave a stupid penalty against us, to lying on the bathroom floor at night feeling like nothing mattered. All in one day. Coach Joseph found me in the changing room after lunch, fists clenched. He didn't tell me to calm down. He just stood with me and said, "That call was unfair. You're allowed to be furious. Just not at the wall." That night I told my dad about the bathroom floor. He sat with me for a long time and said we'd keep talking, and if the low days kept coming, we'd see the school counsellor together.

qa.q: What made Anand want to punch a wall?
qa.a: The ref gave a stupid penalty against the team.

qa.q: How did Anand feel that night?
qa.a: Anand felt low, as if nothing mattered, after a day of joy and rage.

qa.q: What did Coach Joseph and Anand's dad do that helped?
qa.a: The coach named the unfairness and set a limit on hitting; the dad sat with Anand that night and planned to see the counsellor if the lows continued.

qa.q: What is it like for Anand's dad to hear about the bathroom floor?
qa.a: He is likely worried and caring, choosing to stay close and keep talking.

grounding: Shows a teen with intense highs and lows in one day, supported by steady adults who stay close.

passage:
Monday: Hemant came home grinning because Lavanya had laughed at his joke. He blasted music and helped cook dinner.
Tuesday: The class trip was cancelled because of a few boys' behaviour, and Hemant raged at the unfairness, slammed his door and told his mother, Vasudha, that she didn't understand anything. She said calmly, "I'll be in the kitchen when you're ready."
Thursday: He barely spoke, lying on his bed with red eyes, saying he felt sad for no reason. Vasudha sat on the floor beside the bed and stayed. "Big feelings at your age are normal. And I'm here for all of them." Later he came out and asked for chai.

qa.q: Why was the class trip cancelled?
qa.a: Because of a few boys' behaviour.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel on Thursday?
qa.a: He felt sad for no clear reason, lying quietly with red eyes.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that kept Hemant connected?
qa.a: She stayed calm, gave him space when angry and sat with him when sad, telling him she was there for all of it.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel when Hemant says she doesn't understand anything?
qa.a: Vasudha is probably stung, but she stays calm and keeps the door open.

grounding: Shows over a week a teen's intense highs and lows, with a steady parent who stays close.

passage:
Sit, Mehak, you look like the sky is falling. Let me tell you about Alka, my friend from school, back when I was sixteen too.
One Monday Alka came skipping into class because a boy had smiled at her at the bus stop. By lunch she was shouting at our maths teacher over a mark she felt was unfair. By evening she was crying behind the water tank, sure nobody in the world understood her.
I thought she was going mad. But her grandmother, a quiet lady who sold pickles, just sat with her on the steps every evening that month. No lectures. She'd say, "Storms pass, beta. Eat something first."
Alka grew into the steadiest nurse I know. So no, you're not broken, Mehak. You are sixteen, and your Nani is right here on these steps.

qa.q: Where did Alka cry in the evening?
qa.a: She cried behind the water tank.

qa.q: How did Alka feel within that one Monday?
qa.a: She swung from giddy and excited in the morning to angry at an unfair mark at lunch to lonely and sad by evening.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Alka through that month?
qa.a: Her grandmother chose to sit with her every evening without lectures, giving her a steady adult presence while the storms passed.

qa.q: How did Alka's grandmother see Alka's storms?
qa.a: She seemed to see them as passing weather to sit through calmly, not as a problem to scold.

grounding: Nani tells Mehak about a friend whose teenage highs and lows within one day were eased by a steady adult, showing such swings are often normal.
